tutorialHtml:
DENIZ AKKABAK · SEEDANCE 2.0 TUTORIAL · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

The Wrong Size

Directing a cinematic sneaker commercial in Seedance 2.0 — one absurd image of a man hauling a giant shoe through an Italian street becomes a four-scene ad with dialogue, product logic and an end card.

A TUTORIAL BY DENIZ AKKABAK · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

MODEL SEEDANCE 2.0 FORMAT 16:9 · 15S · 4 SCENES GENRE COMEDY COMMERCIAL

Great commercials are built on one absurd, instantly readable premise. Here it is a size complaint taken literally: the shoe is simply too big, so the customer carries it — all of it — to the store and asks for a smaller one. One reference image supplies everything: the man, the product, the street and the crowd. One prompt turns it into a four-scene spot with real dialogue, believable physics and a particle-logo end card. Below: the reference, the verbatim prompt, and the anatomy of why it sells.

STEP 01

The Reference — One Image, Whole Campaign

This generation uses a single reference, and the prompt names it what it is: the master scene and single source of truth. The image carries four jobs at once — the actor's identity (face, curls, sunglasses, outfit), the hero product (the giant sneaker, its colors and side-panel logo), the location (the narrow sunlit Italian street), and even the supporting cast of amazed tourists. When one image locks everything, every cut in the ad has an anchor to return to.

REFERENCE 1 — THE MASTER SCENE (SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH)

Set Seedance 2.0 to 16:9 and 15 seconds, attach this image as the only reference, then paste the prompt below unchanged.

STEP 02

SEEDANCE 2.0 · 16:9 · 15S · 4 SCENES · DYNAMIC CUTS

FORMAT: 15s / 16:9 horizontal / cinematic sneaker commercial / dynamic cuts, 4 scenes

STYLE: Hollywood live-action commercial, ARRI Alexa LF aesthetic, 35mm film look, clean rectilinear lenses, natural perspective, shallow depth of field, natural Italian daylight, warm stone tones, professional color grading, real-world physics, subtle film grain.

REFERENCE:

Reference 1 = master scene and single source of truth: the curly-haired man with black square sunglasses, cream tee, beige trousers and plain white sneakers, carrying the giant grey sneaker on his back through the narrow Italian street. Preserve his exact face, hair, beard and sunglasses in every shot; sunglasses always on. Preserve the giant sneaker's exact design, colors and logo; the smaller pair he tries on later is the identical model at normal foot size. Match this street and bystanders.

VIDEO PROMPT:

0-4s: The man walks down the sunlit cobblestone street bent under the giant sneaker, heavy realistic weight in his steps, tourists watching amazed. Slow lateral tracking beside him, then cut to a reverse angle over the shoulders of tourists raising phones as he passes toward the wooden shop doorway on the right.

4-7s: The giant shoe jams in the doorframe. He plants his feet and shoves it through with two hard pushes, scraping and squeezing past the frame with believable friction, then he slips in behind it.

7-10s: Cut to the shop interior: a bright minimal sneaker store, light wooden shelves of grey and white running shoes, travertine counter, warm spotlights. He gestures at the giant sneaker beside him and tells the smiling staff member in a cream tee: "This one's a bit big. Could I get it in a smaller size?" She replies warmly: "Of course, sir." Both speak natural American-accented English.

10-13s: Cut to him seated on a wooden store bench, now wearing the same sneaker model at normal size, pulling the final lace knot tight in close-up. He stands, checks his feet and says happily: "This fits perfectly. Thank you so much."

13-15s: Cut to clean end card: fine glowing particles sweep in and assemble into the same black logo seen on the giant sneaker's side panel, centered on a light background. Hard stop.

CAMERA: Smooth natural cinematic coverage; lateral tracking and over-shoulder reverse on the street, static medium two-shot for the dialogue, macro close-up on the lace knot, slow push-in on the logo. No handheld chaos, no distorted wide lenses.

SFX: No music. Italian street ambience, distant chatter, footsteps on stone, fabric shifting under the shoe's weight, wood creak and rubber squeak at the door, quiet store room tone, lace pull and knot cinch, soft particle shimmer on the logo. Dialogue clear and natural.

NEGATIVE PROMPT: no music, no fisheye, no vignette, no lens distortion, no cartoon, no unrealistic physics, no floating objects, no identity change, no face distortion, no sunglasses removal, no shoe redesign, no logo distortion, no extra text, no captions, no watermarks.

STEP 03

Anatomy — Why the Spot Sells

  1. 1

    The contract

    FORMAT declares a commercial with dynamic cuts and exactly four scenes — so Seedance paces the fifteen seconds like an ad, not like a continuous vlog.

  2. 2

    Ad-grade style

    STYLE swaps the usual phone-realism trick for polished cinema language: clean rectilinear lenses, shallow depth, warm stone tones, professional grade. A commercial is allowed to look expensive.

  3. 3

    Single source of truth

    The REFERENCE block does the heavy lifting: identity locked with sunglasses always on, the product's design and logo frozen, and one crucial sentence — the smaller pair is the identical model at normal size. That line is the whole product story.

  4. 4

    Physics as comedy

    The gag is played straight: heavy realistic weight in his steps, the shoe jamming in the doorframe, two hard pushes with believable friction. The absurd premise earns its laugh through mundane physics, not cartoon logic.

  5. 5

    Directed dialogue

    Both lines are written verbatim with accent and tone notes. Scripted speech pins the timing of scenes 3 and 4 and gives the model exact lip-sync targets instead of improvised mumbling.

  6. 6

    The end card

    Scene 5 in disguise: particles assembling into the logo from the shoe's side panel is a classic commercial close — and because the logo comes from the reference image, no text generation is risked.

  7. 7

    The insurance

    NEGATIVE PROMPT guards the ad's fragile parts: no shoe redesign, no logo distortion, no sunglasses removal, no extra text — every clause protects either the product or the star.

THE RESULT

Output — Fifteen Seconds, Sold

Score it like a client would: the weight reads in his back on every step, the doorframe beat lands with real friction, the store dialogue is clean and warm, the normal-size pair matches the giant one stitch for stitch, and the particle logo closes it with a hard stop. One image, one prompt, one airable spot.

ONE IMAGE. ONE PROMPT. ONE AD.

Absurd premise, straight face, real physics — that's a commercial.

Swap the sneaker for a watch, a bottle or a sofa: stage one master image that locks actor, product and place, then write four timed scenes around a literal-minded gag. The single-source-of-truth method carries any product you can carry.
